newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu seeks cabinet approval for PLO deal.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu seeks cabinet approval for PLO deal.

text.p: Israel put extra troops in Hebron on Wednesday to thwart Jewish settler protests after sealing a deal with the PLO to withdraw from most of the city.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat bowed to intense U.S. political pressure and clinched the long-delayed Hebron accord at an overnight summit. They also agreed Israel would complete three further pullbacks in the West Bank over the next 18 months.

Netanyahu brought the agreement to his cabinet on Wednesday which seemed likely to approve it, although up to seven of the 18 ministers could oppose it. Arafat was also scheduled to put the still unpublished accord to his cabinet on Wednesday night.
U.S. mediators lit cigars like proud fathers after the tense talks at the Erez crossing between Israel and PLO-ruled Gaza.
But Arafat and Netanyahu did not seem overjoyed by the birth of an accord that will give the PLO less land than it demanded and has caused a right-wing revolt in Israel's Likud-led coalition.
The two leaders were stern-faced. They briefly shook hands but did not speak to reporters. Palestinians said Netanyahu insisted the initialling of the accord be held out of sight of the cameras.
The accord was an ideological wrench for Netanyahu and the Likud who had vowed never to cede part of the biblical Land of Israel to Palestinians.

"I think it is a very sad moment, for the world, for the country, for the city," said Hebron settler leader Noam Arnon. "Arafat, who is still managing a terror organisation, signed an agreement with Netanyahu who wrote a book against terrorism."

Chief Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas told Reuters the deal requires Israel to withdraw its troops from 80 percent of Hebron within 10 days and implement the first of three subsequent West Bank redeployments by March 7.

"We are glad we have finalised the Hebron deal. It is the first agreement we have signed with the Likud. We hope this will be the beginning of more deals with this government," said Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen.
Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said one of the most important achievements for Israel was a letter of guarantees to Netanyahu from outgoing U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.

Naveh told Israel Radio the letter stated that Israel would define the depth of the three additional West Bank pullbacks. Palestinians have long thought they would eventually control up to 90 percent of the West Bank but Netanyahu has lowered such expectations.
U.S. ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk told the radio the size of the areas to be handed to the PLO in the three subsequent redeployments "is, according to the agreement, Israel's decision".

Israeli security sources said police and soldiers had been deployed in Hebron to prevent unrest ahead of the pullback from the town. Hebron, where some 400 militant Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Arabs, is a flashpoint of violence.

The sources said the army needed about 48 hours to complete the withdrawal to the 20 percent of the city that Israel will retain. Some sources expected the redeployment after the Israeli parliament votes on the agreement on Thursday.
U.S. mediator Dennis Ross said the agreement included a "note for the record" which dealt with the future Israeli redeployments from the West Bank and other non-Hebron related issues.

"These two documents represent a very important building block in terms of developing the relations between the two sides and in terms of laying out a pathway of greater hope and the possibility for peace in the Middle East," he said.
Palestinian officials said Israelis and Palestinians spelled out commitments to each other in another section of the agreement titled "Agreed Minutes" but refused to disclose its contents.
